questions.prompt: You speak to one friend. Complete: "Be careful with the knife! Don't cut ___."
questions.explanation: The friend would cut the same person who holds the knife, so we need a reflexive pronoun. You speak to ONE person, so the form is "yourself"; "yourselves" is for several people.

questions.prompt: What do we call a person who drives a taxi?
questions.explanation: In a compound noun the main word comes last: the person is a driver (drive + -er), and "taxi" says what kind, so "a taxi driver". "A driver taxi" copies the word order of French or Arabic, where the main word comes first.

questions.prompt: Answer: "Sara speaks English very well." Which question word asks about "very well"?
questions.explanation: "Very well" describes the manner, and "how" asks about manner: How does Sara speak English? "Why" would ask for a reason and "when" for a time.

options.text: Tom is tall whereas his brother is tall too.
Tom is tall whereas he plays basketball.
Tom is tall whereas his brother is very tall.
Tom is tall whereas his brother is short.

questions.explanation: "Whereas" joins two opposite ideas: tall and short are opposites, so the contrast is real. When both brothers are tall there is no contrast (use "and"), and playing basketball is not the opposite of being tall.

questions.prompt: The books belong to my two brothers. Complete: "These are my ___ books."
questions.explanation: There are two brothers, so the noun is plural and already ends in -s: we only add the apostrophe, "my brothers' books". "Brother's" would mean one brother, and a plural in -s never takes a second s.

"Swim" is a short verb ending in one vowel + one consonant, so the consonant doubles: swimming. "Write" and "come" end in a silent e, which drops (writing, coming), and "wait" has two vowels before the t, so nothing doubles (waiting).
